sents: In my second year as a waller I built forty metres along the top of a hill farm, and I was proud of it.
The joints were tight and the courses ran level.
After one wet winter a stretch of it bellied out like a full sack.
I took the fault to be in the face stones, and rebuilt the stretch with heavier ones.
The next spring it bellied again.
An older waller who was passing pulled a single face stone out of it and put his arm into the wall up to the elbow.
There was nothing behind the stone.
I had thrown the small stones into the middle loose, as filling, and they had settled.
A dry-stone wall fails from the inside.
The faces are what a walker sees, and the hearting, the small stones packed between them, is what holds the faces up.
Each of those stones has to be placed and wedged by hand, and every metre or so a long stone has to run through the wall and tie the two faces together.
I have built that way for twenty years, and none of those walls has moved.

batches.assembled_prompt:
The text, each paragraph starting with its number:

[P1] In my second year as a waller I built forty metres along the top of a hill farm, and I was proud of it. The joints were tight and the courses ran level. After one wet winter a stretch of it bellied out like a full sack.

[P2] I took the fault to be in the face stones, and rebuilt the stretch with heavier ones. The next spring it bellied again. An older waller who was passing pulled a single face stone out of it and put his arm into the wall up to the elbow. There was nothing behind the stone. I had thrown the small stones into the middle loose, as filling, and they had settled.

[P3] A dry-stone wall fails from the inside. The faces are what a walker sees, and the hearting, the small stones packed between them, is what holds the faces up. Each of those stones has to be placed and wedged by hand, and every metre or so a long stone has to run through the wall and tie the two faces together. I have built that way for twenty years, and none of those walls has moved.

Score each sentence on the five offences below. A score is roughly how many readers in ten would meet the problem at that sentence (0 = none, 9 = nearly all).

1. Total: for a sentence that allows no exception (no, nobody, none, never, always, every, all, cannot, only, the one, the whole), score 0 to 9 how likely a reader is to think at once of a plain exception and doubt the sentence for it.
2. Defensive: score 0 to 9 how likely a reader is to wonder at this sentence whom it is answering, because it defends against or denies something nobody has said.
3. Glib: score 0 to 9 how likely a reader is to find this sentence glib: a confident line that sounds settled and says less than it seems to, or a line shaped as a saying where a plain statement belongs, two clauses joined by "and" or "so" that each say what, where or how a thing is, as in "The kitchen is where a restaurant is made, and the menu is how it is sold"; nearly every reader hears that shape, whatever the line says. A quotation, a saying offered as one, or verse does not count.
4. Explained to: score 0 to 9 how likely a reader is to feel talked down to at this sentence, because it tells them what any adult already knows or can see for themselves.
5. Lowered standing: score 0 to 9 how likely a reader is to take the author less seriously at this sentence because the author lowers their own standing to speak on the point.

Spelling and grammar do not count.

Write a TSV and nothing else. One row per sentence where any offence scores 2 or more, in reading order: paragraph.sentence (e.g. 3.2), TAB, the five scores comma-separated in the order above, TAB, why: what the reader meets at this sentence, in at most 15 words. Describe the stumble, not a way to fix it. Where total (1) scores 4 or more, the why names the exception the reader thinks of. Last line: END.

3.why: The author's own wall failing invites doubt about his skill so far.

7.why: Loose filling stones were there, settled lower, so "nothing" overstates.

9.why: A settled maxim, though walls also fail at footings or through frost.

10.why: "What a walker sees… what holds" saying shape; faces being visible is obvious.

11.why: "Each" stone hand-placed sounds absolute for every hearting stone in a wall.

12.why: In twenty years, surely one wall was hit by livestock, tractors or frost heave?
